messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Clergy/Pastor
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Affective Expression: Crying, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hopelessness: I have no future, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rekha is a 47-year-old South Asian woman who, until two years ago, served as a pastor in a small, tight-knit congregation in a Midwestern city. She is divorced, lives alone, and has not led a service or counseled a single parishioner since the night she was abducted from the church parking lot following an evening prayer meeting. The men who took her—three of them, though the number sometimes shifts in her mind—held her for four days in a basement. They demanded she renounce her faith publicly, and when she refused, they used what was at hand: a length of electrical cord, a rusted pipe, and days without food or water. She remembers the cord. She remembers the pipe. But there are hours that are simply gone, erased, and other moments that replay with a clarity that makes her gag.

What Rekha cannot escape, no matter how carefully she manages her life, is a taste. It is the taste of the cloth they forced into her mouth, something oily and metallic that she now encounters at unpredictable moments—biting into a piece of bread, drinking tap water, even brushing her teeth. When the taste surfaces, her body reacts before her mind can catch up: her throat closes, her hands go cold, and she is certain, absolutely certain, that she is back in that basement, even though she knows she is standing in her own kitchen. She has come to believe that she cannot trust her own body’s signals. Even when her closest friend tells her she is safe, Rekha finds it impossible to believe. Safety, she has concluded, is a word that applies to other people.

In the months after her release, Rekha tried to return to her calling. She stood in the pulpit once. She saw a man in the third row who had a similar build to one of her captors, and her mind went blank. She could not remember the scripture she had prepared. She could not remember how to breathe. She stepped down and has not gone back. She now believes she is no longer capable of the work that defined her. The thought of counseling someone in distress fills her with a specific dread: that she will begin to cry, and that if she starts crying, she will not be able to stop. She has learned to suppress any thought of the event before it can fully form. When a memory threatens to surface, she physically shakes her head, or gets up and walks to another room. The strategy works in the moment, but it has hollowed out her days. She no longer answers phone calls from the congregation. She has stopped reading her email. Her life has narrowed to a small apartment and a set of rigid routines.

Eating has become a battleground. Rekha restricts her food intake with a precision that feels like the only thing she still controls. She eats the same three foods, prepared the same way, at the same times each day. Any deviation risks that taste, and that taste risks everything. She has lost weight. Her doctor has expressed concern. Rekha does not explain why.

She is hypervigilant toward people in a way that exhausts her. She scans every face when she goes to the grocery store. She watches hands. She watches exits. She has left a full cart in the aisle because a man in a brown jacket walked past her. She knows this is not sustainable. She knows she is not living. But when she tries to explain it to herself, what she feels most acutely is guilt. She remembers fragments—the pipe, the taste, a single clear image of a crack in the ceiling—and she is flooded with the conviction that she should have been stronger, that she should have done something differently, that she somehow deserved what happened because she failed to prevent it.

What finally brought Rekha to seek help was not her own suffering but a letter from the church board, asking if she would consider an official leave of absence. The letter was kind. It was patient. It had been written six months ago, and she had not opened it until last week. When she read it, she understood that she had been waiting for someone else to name what she already knew: that she has no future. She cannot see a version of herself that leads a congregation again. She cannot see a version of herself that eats a meal without fear. She came to therapy because she is afraid of what will happen if she does not—and because, beneath the fear, there is a small, stubborn part of her that still believes in the possibility of being restored.
